My bMail identity
Manage identifiability, privacy mode, and verification channels
Identifiable anonymity explained
Anonymous mode
Email name is a pseudonym (19902301). Receivers cannot identify your real name. However, bgmail.com domain certifies identifiability — you can be contacted through the ISP if needed.
Real name mode
Email name shows your real name (j.park). Receivers recognize you instantly. Certification by KT Telecom adds a second layer of trust beyond the name alone.
Both modes
The bMail domain name (bgmail.com) always signals identifiability — regardless of the email name. Domain cannot be spoofed at the transport layer (DKIM/SPF/DMARC).

bCA operator portal —
Certify bMail identities using existing subscriber data · Zero-copy policy enforced
Certificate issuance process
1
User applies at bMail ISP
User selects this bCA and grants permission to use subscriber data for certification only (a signed consent token, granted here).
2
ISP sends certification request
Request includes bMail address and permission token. No personal data flows to ISP.
3
bCA verifies via subscriber DB
Identity confirmed against its own records. Pseudonyms allowed — only the domain must be certified.
4
Signed certificate issued
Certificate token returned to ISP. ISP marks the bMail ID as identifiable. Personal data stays at the bCA.

How to interpret a bMail address
Legitimate bMail (real name)
efraim.turban@bgmail.com
Real name + certified domain. Sender is identifiable by name and domain certification.
Legitimate bMail (anonymous)
19905217@bgmail.com
Pseudonym name + certified domain. Sender is anonymous but domain guarantees identifiability.
Not a bMail address
efraim.turban@gmail.com
Real name but non-certified domain (gmail.com ≠ bgmail.com). Display name could be fake.

Trust flow visualizer
Step through the four core bMail protocols — Identifiability · Verification · Sustainability · Changeability
Identifiability flow — A receiver requests confirmation that a bMail sender is genuinely identifiable
Receiver
→
bMail ISP
→
Sender (notified)
→
bCA (Telco/Bank)
→
Receiver (certified)
1
Receiver submits identification request
Receiver asks: "Is j.park@bgmail.com a genuine identifiable sender?" Request submitted via bMail ISP portal.
2
ISP validates request and notifies sender
ISP checks request legitimacy, then notifies the sender (j.park) for their permission to proceed with identification.
3
Sender reviews and approves
Sender decides whether to allow identification. If approved, ISP requests a certificate from the selected bCA (KT Telecom).
4
bCA issues certificate — delivered to receiver
Signed certificate confirms sender is identifiable. Personal data stays at bCA. Sender is notified of the disclosure event.
Verification flow — Receiver suspects their email came from a compromised or phishing account
Receiver (suspicious)
→
bMail ISP
→
Genuine sender (backup channel)
→
Receiver (protected)
1
Receiver flags suspicious email
Email appears to come from h.lee@bgmail.com but content is suspicious. Receiver reports to ISP — NOT by replying to the email.
2
ISP contacts sender via backup channel
ISP sends verification message to h.lee's registered KakaoTalk ID. The potentially compromised email address is never used in this step.
3
Genuine sender confirms or denies
If sender denies sending the email: phishing confirmed. Sender immediately changes password. ISP notifies receiver that the email was fraudulent.
4
Both parties protected — incident logged
Receiver avoids the phishing link. Sender recovers account. ISP logs the incident. Generative AI / deepfake phishing attempts are neutralised by this backup-channel design.
Sustainability flow — Lifelong bMail ID persists across institutional changes
User (graduates)
→
Institution deactivates edu email
→
bMail ISP (ID persists)
→
All platforms remain connected
1
University deactivates jpark@univ.edu
Student graduates. Institutional email is terminated per university policy — a common occurrence documented across institutions (University of Minnesota, 2024).
2
bMail ID j.park@bgmail.com remains active
The bMail ISP guarantees lifelong service. The bMail ID is independent of any institutional affiliation. No disruption to the user's primary identifier.
3
E-commerce platforms remain reachable
Coupang, Naver Shopping, and other platforms registered under j.park@bgmail.com continue to function normally. No broken member IDs, no lost customer relationships.
4
Analogous to ORCID iD for researchers
Like a Persistent Identifier (PID), the bMail ID ensures continuity of identity across systems — with the added benefit of global communicability.
Changeability flow — Secure protocol to update a platform member ID when the old email expires
User
→
bMail ISP
→
bCA verifies identity
→
ISP issues change token
→
Platform updates record
1
User requests ID change at bMail ISP
Old ID: jpark@univ.edu (expired). New ID: j.park@bgmail.com. User selects platforms to update.
2
ISP requests identity re-verification from bCA
KT Telecom confirms the user is the legitimate owner of both the old and new IDs. No fraudulent substitution is possible.
3
ISP generates and transmits a signed change token
Cryptographically signed token contains old ID, new ID, bCA confirmation, and timestamp. Transmitted to each selected platform via secure protocol.
4
Platform verifies token and updates member record
Old ID remapped to new bMail ID. All purchase history, reviews, loyalty points, and preferences are preserved. Zero duplicate-ID risk. Platforms like Naver and KakaoTalk that currently prohibit ID changes (Inquivix, 2023; Naver, 2025) can enable this through the bMail protocol.
System architecture
Stakeholder roles and interactions — based on Figure 3, Anonymous (2025)
bMail User
  • Registers bMail ID at ISP (real name or anonymous)
  • Selects bCA and grants identity permission
  • Provides backup verification channels
  • Approves or rejects identification requests
  • Registers on platforms using bMail ID
  • Initiates ID-change protocol when needed
bMail ISP
  • Issues bMail domain names (bgmail.com etc.)
  • Enforces authentication (DKIM/SPF/DMARC/ARC)
  • Lists certified domains on public portal
  • Manages identification service (with user approval)
  • Routes verification via backup channels
  • Issues signed ID-change tokens to platforms
  • Monitors propagation and blocks fake domains
  • Never stores personal data (zero-copy)
bCA (Certification Authority)
  • Holds genuine identity data (telco, bank, govt)
  • Issues signed certificate tokens to ISP
  • Personal data never transmitted to ISP
  • Certifies pseudonyms and real names alike
  • Verifies identity for ID-change requests
  • Annual certificate renewal
bMember Platform
  • Recognises bMembers as identifiable customers
  • Implements secure ID-change protocol with ISP
  • Tags reviews by author certification status
  • Reduces fake reviews and fake accounts
  • Retains customers through lifelong bMail IDs
  • Gains social responsibility reputation
